doc.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Three D's and Bay Area struggles
title: Listing himself as a teacher to get a telephone
summary: Jazz musicians were last on the phone priority list, so Iola's friend advised putting down teacher.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Okay. Listen on the headphones. If we need to stop . . . If you look at the 1949 phone book for San Francisco and you look under Paul Desmond, you see that he’s listed as a music teacher. So it’s clear that Paul took students around this time. Did you do that as well? Did you take any piano students?
We all discovered that if we put down “jazz musician,” we’d never get a phone.
So we were months and months and months trying to call the company. They’d always make up some excuse. One of the Mills girls lived downstairs on 18th Street. Who was that?

Bert Corvello, music major from Mills. Worked at the telephone company. She said, “They will never give a jazz musician, or even maybe a musician, a phone. You’ll be last on the list, and the list is long. Put down ‘teacher’.”
This was shortly after World War II, and there really was a priority list about who got a telephone.
And jazz musicians were at the bottom of the list.
At the bottom of the list.
